name: Reconstructive Plastic Surgery, Skin Grafts, Flaps, and Tissue Expansion

reference.source: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd ed / Mathes and Nahai Classification
clinicalPearls: The reconstructive ladder progresses from primary closure to skin grafts, local flaps, regional flaps, and free microvascular transfer
Skin graft take progresses through three distinct phases: plasmatic imbibition (0-48h), inosculation (48-72h), and revascularization
Full-thickness skin grafts experience less secondary contracture and provide better color match than split-thickness grafts
Axial pattern flaps incorporate an anatomically named direct cutaneous arteriovenous system with superior reliable dimensions
Deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) free flap preserves rectus abdominis muscle while providing autologous breast reconstruction
reference.pathophysiology: Skin graft survival depends on direct contact with a well-vascularized recipient bed free of infection (bacterial count < 10^5/g) and shear forces. During plasmatic imbibition, nutrients diffuse passively across the fibrin layer. Inosculation establishes direct microvascular connections between recipient and graft capillaries, followed by true neovascular ingrowth. Flaps maintain intrinsic blood supply through pedicled or microvascularly anastomosed vessels, enabling reconstruction across avascular beds, exposed bone, joint capsules, or irradiated tissue.
additionalDifferentials: Seroma or hematoma lifting skin graft versus graft shear failure
Venous congestion of flap versus arterial thrombosis
Hypertrophic scar versus true keloid extending beyond wound margins
Partial-thickness burn necrosis versus full-thickness tissue loss
additionalInvestigations: Handheld acoustic Doppler ultrasound or color duplex for flap pedicle and perforator mapping
Quantitative wound tissue biopsy culture if bacterial contamination exceeds threshold
Near-infrared indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence angiography for intraoperative flap perfusion
Histopathological analysis of scar tissue distinguishing keloid from hypertrophic scar
